items.gist: It distinguishes guru levels across traditions and states that even a Vāma-path knower of supreme truth should be re-initiated in the Bhairava Tantra.
Śaiva, Vaimala, Siddhānta, Ārhata, Kāruka, and especially Vaiṣṇava practitioners are treated as paśus, lacking eligibility in the Bhairava maṇḍala.
Stealing knowledge through deceit requires prāyaścitta, and a guru who imposes such conditions is not a source of śaktipāta.
When a guru is found to act in an inverted manner, his knowledge should be withdrawn and he abandoned, like a king punishing a thief.
Those attached to Vaiṣṇava and similar paths are deluded by Māyā, and violating samaya in both one's own and another's view brings loss.

items.topic: Śiva knowledge not in other śāstras
items.gist: Śiva knowledge does not shine in other śāstras, and lower traditions do not know the unbounded state of the higher.
Higher gurus activate lower functions, and śaktipāta can rapidly elevate a disciple across limited domains.
One who performs unauthorized higher practices becomes punishable, while knowledge progresses from scriptural to contemplative to meditative.
Without supreme meditative knowledge, liberation is not achieved; even yogic attainments in lower tattvas are insufficient.
The guru is defined by cultivated liberating knowledge, and one should choose such a guru while abandoning others.
A knowledge-seeker should move from guru to guru, since a guru lacking śakti cannot yield liberation.
One desiring both enjoyment and liberation should seek a guru with cultivated knowledge and yogic power, preferring a knowledge-giver if needed.
If no single guru is complete, one may gather knowledge from many gurus to form an undivided circle of awareness.
Kallaṭa taught this, and the author studied lower śāstras out of curiosity while not serving non-Śaiva paths.
Progression through traditions is gradual, and one should not doubt the need for multiple gurus.
A guru is authoritative in his own śāstra, while serving a lower guru for higher attainment leads to destruction.
Seeking higher attainment through lower gurus or māyīya śāstras brings destruction and suffering.
One blessed by śaktipāta abandons lower paths, and the Śaiva tradition re-initiates those who have fallen elsewhere.

items.topic: Brahmā and Viṣṇu not in own śāstras
items.gist: Even Brahmā and Viṣṇu did not establish liṅga-rites in their own systems, and Vaiṣṇava teachers initiate some while remaining deluded.
